page: Amazon Web Services c3.2xlarge is a compute-optimized instance powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2680 v2 processor. It features 8 vCPUs mapped to 4 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled, running at a clock speed of 2.8 GHz. The instance is equipped with 15.0 GB of system memory, yielding 1.88 GB per core, and includes 160 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. It operates on the Xen hypervisor with a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps.

Performance benchmarks indicate average multi-core capabilities alongside weaker single-core metrics. The stress-ng multi-core CPU test and Passmark CPU score both fall into the average category, while Geekbench single-core and multi-core scores rank in the poor and weak tiers respectively. Memory bandwidth tests show average performance for both cached and uncached read/write operations. Software compilation with Clang and static web serving throughput also achieve average ratings, whereas cryptographic operations and database tasks perform moderately.

Given its older Intel Xeon architecture, the c3.2xlarge lacks modern instruction sets like AVX-512 and AMX, which limits its efficiency for advanced vector math and machine learning workloads, as evidenced by poor performance in 7B LLM text generation. However, the inclusion of dedicated vCPUs and local NVMe SSD storage provides a stable environment for legacy multi-threaded applications, basic web serving, software compilation, and moderate database operations where dedicated compute is required without the premium cost of current-generation hardware.
description: Amazon Web Services c3.2xlarge is an x86_64 compute-optimized instance utilizing the Xen hypervisor. Powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2680 v2 processor running at 2.8 GHz, it delivers 8 vCPUs across 4 physical cores, supported by 15.0 GB of memory and 160 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. While single-core benchmarks and modern instruction-heavy tasks like LLM text generation rank in the lower percentiles, the instance maintains average performance in multi-core processing, memory bandwidth, and software compilation. Lacking AVX-512 and AMX flags, it is less suited for modern AI workloads but remains a viable, cost-efficient option for legacy multi-threaded applications, static web serving, and moderate database operations requiring dedicated compute resources and local SSD storage.
